The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.

literary_significance: Poems, Chiefly Lyrical introduced the 'Tennysonian' manner that dominated English verse for the next sixty years: the picture of a state of mind held in a landscape, and the perfection of sound. title: Poems (1832)
description: The 1832 volume (dated 1833) containing 'The Lady of Shalott', 'The Palace of Art', 'Oenone', 'The Lotos-Eaters' and 'A Dream of Fair Women' — the volume attacked by John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review in 1833, and the one whose ten years of revision produced the 1842 Poems.

title: Poems (1842)
description: The two-volume Poems of 1842 that ended the ten years' silence: the revised versions of the 1830 and 1832 poems together with 'Morte d'Arthur', 'Locksley Hall', 'Ulysses', 'The Two Voices', 'The Vision of Sin' and 'Break, break, break'.

narrative_structure: It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
principal_characters: Ulysses; King Arthur and Sir Bedivere ('Morte d'Arthur'); the speaker of 'Locksley Hall' and his cousin Amy; St Simeon Stylites; Godiva; Sir Galahad; Lady Clara Vere de Vere; the Lord of Burleigh; Dora; the two voices
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the fourteen-line sonnet, Petrarchan or Shakespearean, and in sequences where the individual sonnets accumulate into a continuous argument or a narrative of feeling. title: The Princess: A Medley
description: Published in 1847 (revised 1850, 1851, 1853, with the intercalated songs added in 1850), a serio-comic poem on the higher education of women: a prince disguises himself as a maid to enter a women's college founded by the princess he is betrothed to.
plot_or_argument: The Prince, betrothed in childhood to the Princess Ida, daughter of King Gama, enters her college in disguise with his friends; discovered, he is wounded, nursed, and the college collapses when Ida's heart is touched by the story of a mother's love; the poem ends with the prince's vision of a reconciled relation between the sexes and with the lyric 'Now sleeps the crimson petal'.
narrative_structure: A prologue and conclusion frame seven cantos of narrative, with six interspersed songs; in blank verse with lyrical interludes.
principal_characters: the Prince; Princess Ida; Cyril; Florian; Psyche; King Gama; the Lady Blanche; Melissa
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for the narrative; the songs in various lyric stanzas ('Tears, idle tears' in a four-line stanza with refrain).
historical_context: The 1840s debate on women's education (Queen's College, London, 1848; the Governesses' Benevolent Institution), the early feminist argument of the English Woman's Journal, and the poem's later embarrassment to its author as the 'woman question' became serious.
literary_significance: The Princess is the Victorian poem on women's education and the most ambitious attempt in verse to argue the case for female intellectual life. Its mixture of comic and serious registers, and its interpolated songs, made it a permanent anthology source, and its reception shows the shift in the debate from comedy to politics inside a single decade.

title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
description: The great elegy of the nineteenth century, begun on the death of Arthur Henry Hallam in Vienna on 15 September 1833 and printed privately in 1849 and published in May 1850: 131 lyric sections in a single stanza, moving from raw grief through the geological and religious crisis of the mid-1840s to a hard-won faith in the 'one far-off divine event'.
plot_or_argument: The sequence is not narrative but seasonal and argumentative: it opens with the yew tree and the funeral, moves through the first Christmas, the springs and winters of the following years, the night reading of the dead friend's letters, the vision of nature as 'red in tooth and claw', the vision of Hallam as a type of the perfected man, and ends with the marriage of Tennyson's sister Cecilia and Edmund Lushington and a benediction on the child to come.
narrative_structure: 131 numbered sections of three or four stanzas, grouped by the anniversaries of Hallam's death and by the seasons; a prologue and an epilogue (the marriage of Cecilia Tennyson).
principal_characters: the elegist; Arthur Henry Hallam (A. H. H.); Cecilia Tennyson and Edmund Lushington, the bride and groom of the epilogue
literary_form: Elegiac sequence in 131 sections and a prologue and epilogue; 'A. H. H.' = Arthur Henry Hallam
meter_and_prosody: The In Memoriam stanza: iambic tetrameter rhymed abba, a closed, echoing quatrain that became the standard English elegiac measure.
historical_context: The 1830s-40s: the Oxford Movement, the geology of Lyell and the 'Vestiges' controversy, the crisis of faith, and the private world of the Tennyson family at Somersby and High Beach; the poem's theology is Broad Church and its science is the new geology.
literary_significance: In Memoriam is the central poem of Victorian doubt and the one work in which the age's scientific and religious crisis is dramatised at full length. It gave the language 'nature, red in tooth and claw' and 'the ringing grooves of change', and its stanza (the 'In Memoriam stanza', abba) became the standard elegiac form of the century. Queen Victoria told Tennyson it was her consolation after the death of Prince Albert.

title: Maud, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1855 and Tennyson's own favourite among his long poems: a monodrama in a variety of metres spoken by a young man driven to madness and murder by his father's ruin, the love of Maud, and the Crimean War.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, ruined by a fraudulent lawsuit against his father, falls in love with Maud, the daughter of his father's enemy; her brother opposes the match, the lovers are discovered, the speaker kills Maud's brother in a duel, and goes mad, imagining himself dead; the poem ends with his recovery and his departure for the Crimean War.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line. A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book.
principal_characters: the unnamed speaker; Maud; Maud's brother; Maud's father; the speaker's father
meter_and_prosody: Eleven sections in varied metres, from lyric tetrameters to a prose-like dramatic speech, with refrains and song fragments.
historical_context: The 1850s: the financial fraud of the period, the 'Maud mania' of the poem's reception, and above all the Crimean War (1853-56), which the poem's ending consecrates as a national redemption. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1855 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice; Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
literary_significance: Maud is the most modern and the most disturbing of Tennyson's long poems: its unstable speaker, its abrupt metrical shifts and its treatment of sexual hysteria and financial ruin make it a key text for the study of Victorian masculinity, and its war ending gave the poem its contemporary scandal. Modern criticism has made it the most discussed of the poems after In Memoriam.

title: Idylls of the King
description: Tennyson's Arthurian epic, published in instalments over twenty-six years — 'Enid' and 'Elaine' (as 'Enid and Nimue') in 1859, 'The Holy Grail' in 1869, 'Gareth and Lynette' and 'The Last Tournament' in 1872, 'Balin and Balan' in 1885 — and dedicated to the memory of Prince Albert.
plot_or_argument: The twelve idylls trace the rise and fall of Arthur's order: the coming of Arthur and the founding of the Round Table; the individual knights' vows and failures (Gareth, Balin, Geraint and Enid, Lancelot, Percivale); the quest of the Holy Grail, which breaks the fellowship; the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere; the rebellion of Mordred and the last battle; and Arthur's passing to Avilion.
narrative_structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

literary_form: Arthurian epic in twelve idylls, in blank verse
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse in the idyll form; each idyll a self-contained narrative episode with its own moral.
historical_context: The Victorian revival of Arthurian matter (the 1839 Eglinton Tournament, the Pre-Raphaelite Arthurian paintings, Malory reprinted in 1817), the empire and its moral mission, and the death of Prince Albert in 1861, which gave the poem a national resonance.
literary_significance: The Idylls are the Victorian age's central myth of empire and of its corruption from within. They made Malory's Arthur a national possession and provided the moral vocabulary of Victorian chivalry, while the poem's increasingly pessimistic later books gave the twentieth century its image of the Victorian imperial self-doubt.

bibliographical_notes: The first four idylls were published by Edward Moxon in July 1859; The Holy Grail and Other Poems followed in 1870, Gareth and Lynette in 1872, and the completed sequence in the collected editions of the 1880s. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Enoch Arden, and Other Poems
description: Published in 1864 and sold 17,000 copies on the day of publication: the story of a fisherman cast away for ten years who returns to find his wife remarried, together with 'The Northern Farmer' dialect poems and 'Aylmer's Field'.
plot_or_argument: Enoch Arden is shipwrecked and lives alone on a desert island for more than ten years; rescued, he returns to find his wife Annie married to his rival Philip, and, unwilling to destroy their happiness, keeps his secret until on his deathbed he confides it to his landlady Miriam Lane. The volume also includes 'The Northern Farmer, Old Style' and 'New Style', dialect monologues, and 'Aylmer's Field', a narrative of avarice and vengeance.
narrative_structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.

The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1864 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under idyll and domestic narrative poem; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
literary_significance: Enoch Arden was the most popular narrative poem of the century and the type of the Victorian verse tale read aloud in the home; it also contains the dialect poems that make Tennyson one of the earliest serious users of regional English speech in verse, a technique taken up by William Barnes and by the twentieth-century regional poets.

title: The Holy Grail and Other Poems
description: Published in 1869, containing 'The Holy Grail', 'The Coming of Arthur', 'The Passing of Arthur' and 'Pelleas and Ettarre': the volume in which the Arthurian epic was given its spiritual centre and its frame.
plot_or_argument: 'The Holy Grail' narrates the Grail vision and the quest that breaks the Round Table, told by Percivale to a monk; 'The Coming of Arthur' establishes the founding myth; 'The Passing of Arthur' narrates the last battle and Bedivere's return of Excalibur.
narrative_structure: A sequence of narrative idylls, each a self-contained story in verse, bound into one continuous argument by the recurring figures and the closing book. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.

Verse narrative in the idyll: blank verse or a regular stanza carries a domestic or rural action told at length, with set-piece description, reported dialogue and a closing reflective passage. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.

title: Becket
description: Published in 1884 and performed at the Lyceum Theatre by Henry Irving on 6 February 1884: Tennyson's most successful play, on the conflict of Henry II and Thomas Becket. It is a dramatic work of 1884 by Alfred Tennyson; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Becket, the king's chancellor turned archbishop, resists Henry's attempt to subject the Church to the royal courts; the conflict over criminous clerks, the exile in France, the return and the murder in the cathedral of 29 December 1170 form the play's structure, and Becket's death is presented as a martyrdom accepted in advance.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Thomas Becket; Henry II; Queen Eleanor; Rosamund de Clifford; John of Salisbury; Herbert of Bosham; Gilbert Foliot; Roger of York; Reginald Fitzurse; Margery
literary_form: Verse tragedy (five acts); victorian verse drama

title: Crossing the Bar
description: Written in October 1889, three years before the poet's death, and printed as the final poem of every collected edition: a prayer for a calm passage at the boundary of life and death, with the Pilot face to face.
plot_or_argument: A short meditation spoken at the moment of departure: the speaker hopes for a tide 'too full for sound and foam', asks that no sadness attend his crossing, and ends with the hope of meeting his 'Pilot face to face'.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation. A sequence of sonnets, each complete in fourteen lines, reading as a continuous argument or a continuous story of feeling when taken in order.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the quatrain. The author's characteristic manner is impeccable vowel music and a metrical inventiveness unmatched in English after Milton.

The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1889 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.

title: Pauline: A Fragment of a Confession
description: Published anonymously at the author's expense in 1833 when he was twenty-one, and withdrawn by him in later life: the confession of a young poet to the woman he loves, tracing his search for a faith through Shelleyan idealism, nature and art.
plot_or_argument: The speaker addresses Pauline across a blank-verse monologue in which he recounts his childhood, his worship of Shelley, his loss of faith, and his discovery that love for her gives him a centre; the poem ends with a vow of fidelity.
narrative_structure: A sequence of monologues, each spoken by a different character in a different scene, with the silent listener implied in every line.
principal_characters: the speaker; Pauline; the Sun-treader (Shelley)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the monologue: a single speaker, not the poet, addresses a silent listener, and the metre is loose enough to carry colloquial interruption, self-betrayal and the aside, while the rhyme scheme holds the argument together. The author's characteristic manner is dramatic monologue with a listener implied but never given voice.
historical_context: The 1830s, the Shelley cult, Byron's death and the decline of the 'Satanic' school, and the young Browning's reading of Shelley, Keats and the French memoirists. The record dates the work as composed in None and first published in 1833 and the corpus places it within The Dramatic Monologue and the Masked Voice, it is catalogued under dramatic monologue and masked lyric; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Pauline is the earliest fully developed dramatic monologue in English in Browning's hand, and its confessional method — a speaker who reveals more than he knows — is the prototype of all his later work.
